entries.clue: Maybe patches up Oxford's medieval road surface? (7)

blocks.note: to mend shoes the way a shoe-repairer does, and an Oxford is a lace-up shoe
the rounded stones laid in old streets

annotation.surface: A tour guide praising the ancient streets of Oxford, the university city.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the city with its old lanes, but in the first sense it is the shoe a cobbler repairs; 'Maybe' flags that an Oxford is just one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: a cobbler cobbles, or patches up, shoes such as Oxfords, and cobbles are also the stones that pave old streets.

entries.clue: Headgear for big characters (4)

blocks.note: hats with a peak
capital letters, as opposed to lower case

annotation.surface: Hats handed out to larger-than-life personalities.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big characters' suggests flamboyant people; here it means capital letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: caps are both hats and, in printers' shorthand, capital letters.

entries.clue: Holiday region may be conjured up in  …  in a seabird's call (8,7)

indicators.note: a conjuror makes things reappear in a new form, as the letters do here

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: A gull's cry on the shore calling up memories of a sunny getaway.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on from the neighbouring clue and add nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the Spanish islands of Majorca, Minorca and Ibiza are among Europe's best-known package-holiday destinations.

entries.clue: Unsophisticated, seeing unexpected creature turning up in lake (2-4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters bottom to top
the piece sits inside the lake

blocks.note: a loch is a Scottish lake
E.T., the film's extraterrestrial, is a creature nobody expects

annotation.surface: Someone naive enough to believe in a monster surfacing from a lake.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points at Nessie in her loch, and the loch really is the lake; the creature is E.T., the film alien.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lo-tech means using simple, unsophisticated technology.

entries.clue: Special unit hides computer program in footwear! (6)

indicators.note: the outer word keeps the other tucked out of sight inside it

blocks.note: the SAS is the British Army's Special Air Service
a bot is an automated program

annotation.surface: An elite squad smuggling software inside boots.
annotation.walkthrough: The SAS is the British special forces regiment, a crossword staple for 'special unit'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: sabots are wooden clogs worn by French peasants, a kind of footwear.

entries.clue: Women's work in underground  river in Wales (7)

blocks.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and his realm
the Taff flows through Cardiff

annotation.surface: Women labouring below ground by a Welsh river, as in a mining valley.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Underground' reads as mining; it is Dis, the classical underworld.
annotation.definitionFit: A transferred sense: the distaff was the stick used in spinning, so it came to stand for women's work and the female side of a family.

entries.clue: Answer to waterworks problem? I'd cure it, possibly (8)

indicators.note: the letters might possibly be arranged another way

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A doctor confidently offering a fix for a urinary complaint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Waterworks' is British slang for the urinary system.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a drug that makes you pass more water is one remedy for a waterworks problem, and the question mark admits the looseness.

entries.clue: Little boxes? (8)

blocks.note: the surface reads small, as in tiny cartons; the setter means young
not containers or fighters but box trees, the evergreen used for hedging

annotation.walkthrough: Box is a hedging tree, so little (young) boxes are SAPLINGS; the question mark owns up to the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: young trees of any kind, box included, are saplings.

entries.clue: Ruddy good place for writer to produce a detective story? (1,5,2,7)

blocks.note: a study is the room where a writer works
ruddy = red, so coloured in scarlet

annotation.surface: An author praising their room as a great place to write crime fiction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' reads as a mild British swear word, but it means red.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Conan Doyle's 1887 novel is the detective story that introduced Sherlock Holmes.

entries.clue: Penalty on account of bad ref I oft rue (10)

indicators.note: the letters are in a bad, disordered state

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A football fan regretting a penalty awarded by a poor referee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penalty' looks like the spot-kick the referee gives; it is the definition in its legal sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal synonym: a forfeiture is the loss of property or rights as a penalty for wrongdoing.

entries.clue: Holy group? Such may be looking to the skies (5)

definitions.text: Such may be looking to the skies

blocks.note: pi is short for pious
a lot = a group, as in 'this lot'

annotation.surface: Devout worshippers gazing heavenwards.
annotation.walkthrough: Looking to the skies sounds like prayer after 'Holy', but it is a flyer scanning the air.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: someone who flies an aircraft keeps watch on the skies.

entries.clue: Unhappy lord outside Parliament finally gives indication of imminent departure (4,5)

indicators.note: the lord goes around the other piece
the last letter is what comes at the end, finally, of Parliament

blocks.note: blue = sad
a peer is a lord
last letter of ParliamenT

annotation.surface: A gloomy peer walking out of the Houses of Parliament.
annotation.walkthrough: The Blue Peter is the blue-and-white flag a ship hoists to show it is about to sail (also a long-running British children's TV show).
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the Blue Peter flag is flown in harbour to signal that a ship will shortly put to sea.

entries.clue: One's snapped after being asked to do this (5,3,6)

definitions.text: One's snapped after being asked to do this

blocks.note: reads as someone breaking or losing their temper; means someone is photographed

blocks.clueFragment: after being asked to do this
blocks.note: the phrase a photographer calls out just before the shutter clicks

annotation.walkthrough: 'Snapped' suggests breaking or losing one's temper; it means photographed.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: photographers traditionally told sitters to look at the camera with this phrase just before taking the picture.

entries.clue: Freakish mare, the pet that has seven feet (10)

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'line that has seven feet'

indicators.note: the letters come out in a freakish order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A monstrous horse kept as a pet, sprouting seven legs.
annotation.walkthrough: Feet are metrical units, not hooves.
annotation.definitionFit: A term from prosody: a line of verse built from seven metrical feet, hepta- being Greek for seven.

entries.clue: English team facing shoot-out ultimately making this? (4)

definitions.text: English team facing shoot-out ultimately making this?

indicators.note: the team stands before, facing, the next piece in the line
ultimately means at the end, so take the end letter of shoot-out

blocks.note: E = English
XI = eleven, a football or cricket side
last letter of shoot-ouT

annotation.surface: England's football side heading for the usual penalty shoot-out.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: England's football teams have so often lost penalty shoot-outs that the whole clue reads straight as a description of going out.

entries.clue: One skilled in words banishing guilt and sin (8)

indicators.note: the letters are sent away and scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A preacher whose words drive out guilt and sin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Banishing' reads as getting rid of the guilt and sin; it tells you to scatter their letters instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: someone who studies or speaks many languages is skilled in words.

entries.clue: Ease of provision (8)

blocks.note: doing something without effort
an amenity or service provided, such as parking or a loan arrangement

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ease of provision' reads as one phrase; split it at 'of' into two meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: facility means both natural ease and an amenity or service provided.

entries.clue: Buy a biography? Do something more interesting! (3,1,4)

blocks.note: a life is a biography, and to get one is to buy it
the dismissive retort to a bore

annotation.surface: A bookseller's suggestion, answered by an exasperated put-down.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal, whimsical reading of the phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: literally acquiring a biography, and the idiom telling someone to stop being dull.

entries.clue: Attempts to restrict naughty lesbians (8)

indicators.note: the tries hold the other word within bounds

blocks.note: tries = attempts
bad = naughty

annotation.surface: Efforts to curb badly behaved women.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' sits by 'lesbians' as if describing them; it is only BAD.
annotation.definitionFit: A dated, literary synonym: tribade, from Greek tribein 'to rub', was an old term for a lesbian.

entries.clue: Not all of you serve an exploitative type (4)

indicators.note: only part of the words is used

blocks.note: yoU SERve

annotation.surface: A remark that only some of you are serving someone who takes advantage.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans the gap between two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a user is someone who exploits others for their own ends.

entries.clue: 'Hang around, girl!', we say, in period of inactivity (6)

indicators.note: the words are spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: hang around = stay; girl = sis(ter)

annotation.surface: Telling a sister to wait about during a dull spell.
annotation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'Stay, sis!' runs together into the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from medicine and politics: stasis is a stoppage, a state where nothing moves or changes.

entries.clue: Gardener's feature in September to April months in Welsh location (6)

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the place

blocks.note: the Gower is a peninsula near Swansea

blocks.clueFragment: feature in September to April months
blocks.note: every month from September to April has an R in its name

annotation.surface: A gardener's favourite plant flowering through the colder months in Wales.
annotation.walkthrough: The R months are the old rule for when to eat oysters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anyone who raises plants is a grower.

entries.clue: Dependent on a number of elements!!! … (14)

definitions.text: Dependent on a number of elements!!!

blocks.clueFragment: Dependent on a number of elements
blocks.note: reads as a plain science phrase: depending on several factors
in maths '!' is the factorial sign, so several of them make a multiple factorial

annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation marks look like mere excitement, but '!' is the mathematical factorial sign.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical term, mostly from genetics: a trait governed by several factors, with the maths pun on top.

entries.clue: Queen, but not our Queen, is someone of original Finnish stock (4)

indicators.note: the named letters are taken away

blocks.note: ESTHER, the biblical queen, minus ER, Elizabeth Regina

annotation.surface: A remark that a certain queen is not ours but a descendant of Finnish people.
annotation.walkthrough: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the British queen.
annotation.definitionFit: An obscure dictionary word: an Esth is an Estonian, a people of Finnic origin.

entries.clue: Time's against jockeys making gallops (9)

blocks.note: T = time
anti = against
to jockey is to vie, jostle for position

annotation.surface: Riders racing the clock on the gallops, a racehorse training track.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jockeys' looks like the riders; it is the verb, jostling for position.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaic synonym: a tantivy is a headlong gallop, the word imitating hoofbeats or a hunting horn.

entries.clue: Tricks of one who proved Fermat's last theorem (5)

definitions.text: one who proved Fermat's last theorem

blocks.note: cunning ploys or stratagems

blocks.clueFragment: one who proved Fermat's last theorem
blocks.note: the British mathematician Andrew, who proved it in 1994

annotation.walkthrough: 'Fermat's last' looks as if it wants a final letter; it is the famous theorem.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: crafty tricks, and the surname of Sir Andrew, who proved the theorem.

entries.clue: Fashion again using nasty polyester, not half poor (7)

indicators.note: something nasty has been messed up, so the letters are left in a mess
those letters are left out
half of a four-letter word is two letters, here the front two

blocks.note: the material, before anything is taken away
the first half of POor, removed from POLYESTER to leave LYESTER

annotation.surface: Remaking clothes from cheap synthetic fabric that is still rather shabby.
annotation.walkthrough: Remove the first half of 'poor' from POLYESTER before rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: re- means again, and to style is to fashion or shape.

entries.clue: Mark gets caught, snitch in school (7)

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the school

blocks.note: c = caught, in cricket scoring
a rat is an informer
sch. = school

annotation.surface: Mark, a pupil, is caught out as the class telltale.
annotation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a boy's name; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a scratch is a thin mark scored on a surface, and both words are nouns here.
